Transcript: So today I want to talk about something that's sitting in almost every kitchen cupboard: food sealed in a can or a jar. Most people assume this was invented in a laboratory, that scientists first worked out what makes food go bad and then designed a way to stop it. It's a nice, tidy story. It's also backwards, and the way it really happened tells us something about how discoveries get made.

Let's go back to France in the seventeen nineties. The country was at war, and its soldiers and sailors had a serious problem. Fresh food rotted long before it could be eaten. Salted meat and hard biscuits lasted, but people got sick living on them for months. So the government offered a large cash prize to anyone who could find a better way to keep food.

The person who solved it wasn't a scientist at all. His name was Nicolas Appert, and he was a sweet maker in Paris, someone who spent his days boiling sugar and fruit. Appert had no theory. What he had was patience. He packed food into thick glass bottles, the heavy kind used for wine, pushed the corks in tight, sealed them with wax, and then set the bottles in boiling water. Then he waited, opened them weeks or months later, and wrote down what he found.

Here's the interesting part. He kept this up for roughly fifteen years. Peas needed one heating time, meat needed another, fruit another. If he heated a bottle too briefly, the food spoiled. If a cork let in even a little air, the food spoiled. Bit by bit, food by food, he built up a set of rules that worked, without ever knowing why they worked. Around eighteen ten he won the prize, and part of the deal was that he had to publish everything in a book, so anyone could copy his method.

So did the scientists step in at this point and explain it? Some tried. One of the leading chemists in France examined the bottles and announced that the answer was air. Keep the air out, he said, and food can't decay. It sounded convincing, and for a long time nobody could show otherwise.

It was wrong. About fifty years later, Louis Pasteur showed that food spoils because of microbes, living things far too small to see, which drift through the air and multiply in food. Appert's boiling killed the microbes already inside the bottle, and his tight seal stopped new ones from getting in. Air on its own, without the microbes, didn't make the food rot. So the explanation came half a century after the method, and the first scientific explanation pointed at the wrong thing.

So when someone tells you that understanding always comes first and useful inventions follow, I'd say be careful. Appert didn't need the theory. He needed careful notes and the stubbornness to open bottle after bottle of spoiled peas. Honestly, I find that more impressive than a lucky flash of insight, because there was no flash. There were just years of small tests.

Transcript: OK, let's get going. Today's question sounds simple. How do ecologists know how many animals live in a place? A lot of people picture a scientist walking around with a clipboard, counting every single animal, one by one. That picture is almost always wrong. For most wild animals, nobody counts them all, because nobody could.

Take the garden snails in the flower beds behind this building. They hide under leaves and stones during the day, they come out mostly at night, and one snail looks a lot like the next. If you tried to count them all, you'd count some twice and miss most of the rest. So instead of counting, ecologists estimate, and one of the oldest ways to do that is called mark and recapture.

Here's how it works. On the first night, you collect, say, forty snails. You put a small dot of white paint on each shell, and you let them go exactly where you found them. Then you wait about a week, so the marked snails have time to mix back in with the others. On the second night you collect again. Let's say this time you find fifty snails, and ten of them have a dot. So one in five of your second catch is marked. If that's true of the whole garden, then your forty marked snails are about one fifth of all the snails, and the garden holds roughly two hundred. Notice how it goes. The fewer marked snails you find the second time, the bigger your estimate gets.

Now, that math only works if a few things are true, and this is where the method runs into its limits. First, the marks have to stay on. If heavy rain wears some of the paint off, you'll find fewer marked snails in the second catch than you really should.

Second, nothing should arrive or leave between the two nights. Snails are slow, so you might think that's easy. But over a week, young snails can hatch, some snails wander off into the next garden, and others get eaten. Song thrushes, for example, are birds that crack snail shells open on stones. A thrush that finds your flower bed can take quite a few snails before your second count.

Third, every snail should be equally easy to catch the second time. If the snails you handled learn to hide deeper, or if you always pick up the ones sitting in the open, your sample isn't fair.

Textbooks usually show this method as one neat line of math, and I think that's a bit misleading. The math is the easy part. The hard part is knowing whether those three conditions held in your garden that week.

So, is mark and recapture reliable for snails? Honestly, that's still an open question. In some experiments, researchers put a known number of snails into a fenced plot and then estimated it. Sometimes the estimate came close. Other times it was off by a third or more, and nobody's fully sure which of the problems caused it. I'm not saying throw the method out. I'm saying treat the number as a careful guess. Next week we'll try it ourselves and see how close we get.

Transcript: So, with exams coming up, I want to talk about something your parents have probably told you a hundred times. Get a good night's sleep, because it helps you remember what you studied. Lots of people believe this, and as far as scientists can tell, it's actually true. The more interesting question is why it's true, and there are two competing explanations.

The first explanation is fairly simple. While you're awake, new things keep coming into your head. Conversations, messages, songs, whatever. Each new thing can push against the memories you made earlier and make them harder to find. Psychologists call this interference. When you're asleep, almost nothing new comes in. So, on this view, sleep doesn't do anything special. It just gives your memories a quiet place to sit, like a sign on a door that says do not disturb.

The second explanation says sleep is much more active than that. While you sleep, the brain goes back over what you learned during the day and makes those memories stronger. This is called consolidation. So sleep isn't just a quiet room. It's more like a night shift, when workers come in and fix up the day's work.

Now, how could we tell these two apart? Here's the interesting part. Researchers have recorded brain cells in rats while the rats ran through a maze. Certain cells fired in a particular order as a rat moved along the path. Later, when the rat was asleep, those same cells fired again, in roughly the same order, and often faster. It looked as if the sleeping brain was running through the maze again. A quiet room doesn't do that.

An even clearer test was done with people. Volunteers learned where about fifty pictures appeared on a computer screen, and each picture came with its own sound. A cat picture came with a meow, for example. Then they took a nap. While they were in deep sleep, the researchers quietly played the sounds for half of the pictures, too softly to wake anyone up. After the nap, people remembered the locations of those pictures better than the locations of the others.

Think about what each explanation predicts here. If sleep only keeps out new information, then every picture should be protected equally. The sounds shouldn't matter. But they did matter, and only for the pictures they belonged to. That's very hard to explain unless the sleeping brain is actively working on particular memories.

So I'd say the evidence supports the second explanation. That doesn't mean interference counts for nothing. Being awake and busy probably does weaken memories a little. It just can't be the whole story.
